  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :

***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean

  [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] {F : C ⥤ D} {G : D ⥤ C} (adj : F ⊣ G) {X Y : C} (f : X ⟶ Y) {Z : C} (h : G.obj (F.obj Y) ⟶ Z) :
  adj.unit.app X ≫ G.map (F.map f) ≫ h = f ≫ adj.unit.app Y ≫ h
```

         L₂                  R₂

CategoryTheory.mateEquiv.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {C : Type u₁} {D : Type u₂} {E : Type u₃} {F : Type u₄}
  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

  (adj₁ : F ⊣ G) (adj₂ : H ⊣ I) : F ⋙ H ⊣ I ⋙ G

  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) → (H ⋙ L₄ ⟶ L₃ ⋙ K) → (G ⋙ L₂ ⋙ L₄ ⟶ (L₁ ⋙ L₃) ⋙ K)

```lean

***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

Given two adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁` and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` both between categories `C`, `D`, there is a
bijection between natural transformations `L₂ ⟶ L₁` and natural transformations `R₁ ⟶ R₂`. This is
defined as a special case of `mateEquiv`, where the two "vertical" functors are identity, modulo
composition with the unitors. Corresponding natural transformations are called `conjugateEquiv`.
TODO: Generalise to when the two vertical functors are equivalences rather than being exactly `𝟭`.

Furthermore, this bijection preserves (and reflects) isomorphisms, i.e. a transformation is an iso
iff its image under the bijection is an iso, see eg `CategoryTheory.conjugateIsoEquiv`.
This is in contrast to the general case `mateEquiv` which does not in general have this property.

  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

***
`F ⋙ G` is the composition of a functor `F` and a functor `G` (`F` first, then `G`).

***
*import Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Functor.Basic*

```lean
CategoryTheory.mateEquiv.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {C : Type u₁} {D : Type u₂} {E : Type u₃} {F : Type u₄}
  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean

Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

defined as a special case of `mateEquiv`, where the two "vertical" functors are identity, modulo
composition with the unitors. Corresponding natural transformations are called `conjugateEquiv`.

Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D

`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

***
Given two adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁` and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` both between categories `C`, `D`, there is a
bijection between natural transformations `L₂ ⟶ L₁` and natural transformations `R₁ ⟶ R₂`. This is
defined as a special case of `mateEquiv`, where the two "vertical" functors are identity, modulo
composition with the unitors. Corresponding natural transformations are called `conjugateEquiv`.
TODO: Generalise to when the two vertical functors are equivalences rather than being exactly `𝟭`.

Furthermore, this bijection preserves (and reflects) isomorphisms, i.e. a transformation is an iso
iff its image under the bijection is an iso, see eg `CategoryTheory.conjugateIsoEquiv`.
This is in contrast to the general case `mateEquiv` which does not in general have this property.

```lean

  {F G : C ⥤ D} {α β : NatTrans F G} (h : α = β) (X : C) : α.app X = β.app X
```

*import Mathlib.CategoryTheory.NatTrans*

```lean

  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean
CategoryTheory.Functor.comp_obj.{v₁, v₂, v₃, u₁, u₂, u₃} {C : Type u₁} [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] {D : Type u₂}
  [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] {E : Type u₃} [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] (F : C ⥤ D) (G : D ⥤ E) (X : C) :
  (F ⋙ G).obj X = G.obj (F.obj X)
```

```lean
CategoryTheory.mateEquiv.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {C : Type u₁} {D : Type u₂} {E : Type u₃} {F : Type u₄}
  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean
CategoryTheory.leftAdjointConjugateSquare.vcomp.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {A : Type u₁} {B : Type u₂}
  {C : Type u₃} {D : Type u₄} [Category.{v₁, u₁} A] [Category.{v₂, u₂} B] [Category.{v₃, u₃} C] [Category.{v₄, u₄} D]
  {G : A ⥤ C} {H : B ⥤ D} {L₁ L₂ : A ⥤ B} {L₃ : C ⥤ D} : (L₂ ⟶ L₁) → (G ⋙ L₃ ⟶ L₂ ⋙ H) → (G ⋙ L₃ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H)
```
***
Composition of a conjugate square with a squares between left adjoints.

```lean
CategoryTheory.rightAdjointConjugateSquare.vcomp.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {A : Type u₁} {B : Type u₂}
  {C : Type u₃} {D : Type u₄} [Category.{v₁, u₁} A] [Category.{v₂, u₂} B] [Category.{v₃, u₃} C] [Category.{v₄, u₄} D]
  {G : A ⥤ C} {H : B ⥤ D} {R₁ R₂ : B ⥤ A} {R₃ : D ⥤ C} : (R₁ ⟶ R₂) → (R₂ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₃) → (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₃)
```

```lean
CategoryTheory.conjugateEquiv.{v₁, v₂, u₁, u₂} {C : Type u₁} {D : Type u₂} [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D]
  {L₁ L₂ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ R₂ : D ⥤ C} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) : (L₂ ⟶ L₁) ≃ (R₁ ⟶ R₂)
```
***
Given two adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁` and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` both between categories `C`, `D`, there is a
bijection between natural transformations `L₂ ⟶ L₁` and natural transformations `R₁ ⟶ R₂`. This is
defined as a special case of `mateEquiv`, where the two "vertical" functors are identity, modulo
composition with the unitors. Corresponding natural transformations are called `conjugateEquiv`.
TODO: Generalise to when the two vertical functors are equivalences rather than being exactly `𝟭`.

Furthermore, this bijection preserves (and reflects) isomorphisms, i.e. a transformation is an iso
iff its image under the bijection is an iso, see eg `CategoryTheory.conjugateIsoEquiv`.
This is in contrast to the general case `mateEquiv` which does not in general have this property.

```lean
CategoryTheory.mateEquiv.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄} {C : Type u₁} {D : Type u₂} {E : Type u₃} {F : Type u₄}
  [Category.{v₁, u₁} C] [Category.{v₂, u₂} D] [Category.{v₃, u₃} E] [Category.{v₄, u₄} F] {G : C ⥤ E} {H : D ⥤ F}
  {L₁ : C ⥤ D} {R₁ : D ⥤ C} {L₂ : E ⥤ F} {R₂ : F ⥤ E} (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) :
  (G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H) ≃ (R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂)
```
***
Suppose we have a square of functors (where the top and bottom are adjunctions `L₁ ⊣ R₁`
and `L₂ ⊣ R₂` respectively).

      C ↔ D
    G ↓   ↓ H
      E ↔ F

Then we have a bijection between natural transformations `G ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H` and
`R₁ ⋙ G ⟶ H ⋙ R₂`. This can be seen as a bijection of the 2-cells:

         L₁                  R₁
      C --→ D             C ←-- D
    G ↓  ↗  ↓ H         G ↓  ↘  ↓ H
      E --→ F             E ←-- F
         L₂                  R₂

Note that if one of the transformations is an iso, it does not imply the other is an iso.

```lean
CategoryTheory.mateEquiv_vcomp.{v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄, v₅, v₆, u₁, u₂, u₃, u₄, u₅, u₆} {A : Type u₁} {B : Type u₂}
  {C : Type u₃} {D : Type u₄} {E : Type u₅} {F : Type u₆} [Category.{v₁, u₁} A] [Category.{v₂, u₂} B]
  [Category.{v₃, u₃} C] [Category.{v₄, u₄} D] [Category.{v₅, u₅} E] [Category.{v₆, u₆} F] {G₁ : A ⥤ C} {G₂ : C ⥤ E}
  {H₁ : B ⥤ D} {H₂ : D ⥤ F} {L₁ : A ⥤ B} {R₁ : B ⥤ A} {L₂ : C ⥤ D} {R₂ : D ⥤ C} {L₃ : E ⥤ F} {R₃ : F ⥤ E}
  (adj₁ : L₁ ⊣ R₁) (adj₂ : L₂ ⊣ R₂) (adj₃ : L₃ ⊣ R₃) (α : G₁ ⋙ L₂ ⟶ L₁ ⋙ H₁) (β : G₂ ⋙ L₃ ⟶ L₂ ⋙ H₂) :
  (mateEquiv adj₁ adj₃) (leftAdjointSquare.vcomp α β) =
    rightAdjointSquare.vcomp ((mateEquiv adj₁ adj₂) α) ((mateEquiv adj₂ adj₃) β)
```
